title: NO KINGS Little Rock
description:
NO KINGS (or Oligarchs or Kleptocrats) Flag Day MARCH for Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion

Join us on Saturday, June 14th at 10:00 AM for the Flag Day March for Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion—a bold, peaceful demonstration across the Broadway Bridge in Little Rock, Arkansas. We march to uplift the voices of the marginalized, to call for justice in our communities, and to affirm that diversity, equity, and inclusion are not optional—they are essential.

📍Meet-up spot: Margaret Clark Adventure Park (Little Rock Riverfront Park) under the Broadway Bridge

🅿️ PARKING INFORMATION:

UNDER THE BROADWAY BRIDGE- This parking location is right next to the meet-up spot and is accessible to those who have mobility needs. 

If you start in front of the Robinson Center, you will go WEST on Markham Street, cross over Broadway Street, and take the first right on Bruce Moore/Arch Street. This street dead-ends at the parking lot.

OTHER PARKING: You are also welcome to park anywhere downtown. If you park downtown near Robinson Center/The Old State House Museum/Doubletree Hotel—
Walk down Conway Street (which runs between Doubletree Hotel and Old State House Museum), over the pedestrian bridge, and that will lead you directly to our meeting spot.

🗓️ SCHEDULE:

9:30AM- Begin gathering at the above Meet-Up spot (more details, maps, and flyers to follow)

10:00AM- Walk across the Broadway Bridge, turn around at NLR Riverfront Park, walk back across the bridge.

~10:45AM- Short Rally @ The Meet-Up Spot

The short rally at the end will include speakers, music, and a united call to action.

🧳 PLEASE BRING:

👟Comfortable shoes
💦 Water!!
☀️Weather-appropriate clothing
🧴Sunscreen
🪧Protest Signs, Flags, and Umbrellas

☂️PROTEST UMBRELLAS:

Decorate an umbrella with protest messages to use as shade!

June 14th also marks Donald Trump’s birthday, a day he has chosen to celebrate with talk of military parades and authoritarian posturing. We reject fear-mongering and exclusion. Instead, we choose unity. While others parade power, we march with purpose. We show the world that our strength lies in compassion, community, and collective action.

We believe that diversity strengthens us, equity uplifts us, and inclusion unites us. Whether you’re marching for racial justice, LGBTQ+ rights, accessibility, gender equity, immigrant protections, or education equity—your voice matters here.

Let’s reclaim June 14th as a day of people power. Together, we march—for a world where everyone belongs.

title: Coffee & Climate Conversation: Honoring Juneteenth — A Conversation About Black Maternal Health
description:
Join us for a special Coffee & Climate Conversation in honor of Juneteenth, featuring a powerful conversation with Stephanie Reese, Moms' Director of Strategic Implementation and Justice, and Almeta Cooper, our National Manager for Health Justice.

In this pre-recorded discussion, we explore the intersection of Black maternal health, pollution burdens in communities of color, and the legacy of Juneteenth. Stephanie and Almeta bring thoughtful perspectives to the conversation—touching on historical context, present-day challenges, and what justice looks like in the fight for clean air and healthy communities.

This conversation uplifts voices and stories that are too often left out—and reminds us that clean air and climate stability are deeply connected to racial and reproductive justice.

Watch on our YouTube channel on June 19th and share with your community.

description:

Cadet Bone Spur is spending millions on a military parade in D.C. This is the first time in U.S. history that a President has made a public spectacle to celebrate his own birthday. You know who does that? Kings.

What To Know:
Not the site of most Everyday Activist events, this is at Shoreline's Park at Town Center, often called "Sculpture Park". Wheelchair-accessible, this ~eight-block strip of grass has a wide, paved path, providing everything we need for this event:
- Rally: UPDATE - we meet at the SOUTH end of the park (Aurora Ave N & N 176th St, near Shoreline City Hall) for a few brief remarks and some chants to rev us up
- March: those who wish to march will be led by Everyday Activists core members proudly bearing a "No Kings" banner
- Sign-waving: those who prefer to stand or sit have lots of space to do so along the perimeter of the park itself, or lining the sidewalk on the opposite side of Aurora (the Fred Meyer side). Feel free to bring a chair.

Transportation, Parking and Bathrooms
- Transportation: We encourage participants to carpool or use public transport. There are Metro bus stops at both ends of the park (N 175th St and N 185th St). Buses also run north and south along Aurora.
- Parking: Is available on side streets between N 175th and N 185th St, but not along Aurora Ave itself. There is limited parking along Midvale Ave, which runs between the park and Shoreline City Hall. It would be nice if we could save those few spaces for people with mobility issues. Please do not park at City Hall. We have paid to use only the park; another event is taking place at City Hall. They have the use of parking there: we do not.

Security
Everyday Activists volunteers will be on hand to provide information, assistance, and basic first aid if needed. Look for the folks in the tasteful yellow safety vests.
accessibility_notes: Bathrooms: There are no public bathrooms, but there are a dozen small businesses in the shopping center adjacent to the park (Starbucks, Orange Julius, etc.). Be prepared to make a small purchase in order to use the facilities.

For bridge protests, where visibility from a distance is crucial, the larger the lettering, the better. Here are some key considerations and general guidelines:
General Visibility Rules:
•	Distance is Key: The primary factor is how far away your audience will be. For highway overpasses, traffic might be moving quickly and at a significant distance.
•	"Rule of Thumb" for Legibility: A common guideline for outdoor signage is that each inch of letter height provides approximately 10 feet of legibility. So, for every 100 feet of viewing distance, you'd want at least 10-inch tall letters.
•	Bridge Specifics: Bridges often mean viewing from a greater distance than a sidewalk. Consider vehicles on the road below, and potentially other onlookers further away.
Practical Recommendations for Bridge Protests:
•	Go Big: Aim for lettering that is at least 12-24 inches tall, and even larger if possible. Some sources suggest using 20x30 or 24x30 inch boards for individual letters to create large, impactful messages.
•	Bold, Simple Fonts: Choose block, sans-serif fonts (like Arial or Helvetica) that are thick and easy to read. Avoid thin, ornate, or script fonts.
•	High Contrast Colors: This is critical!
o	Dark letters on a light background (e.g., black on white, dark blue on yellow) offer the best visibility.
o	Avoid low-contrast combinations like yellow on white or light blue on a pale background.
o	Limit your color palette to two or three colors for maximum impact and clarity.
•	Concise Messaging: Shorter messages with fewer words are easier to read quickly from a distance. Each letter takes up space, so a long message will require smaller letters to fit, reducing visibility.
•	Material and Construction:
o	Sturdy materials: Foam core boards or corrugated plastic are more rigid and durable than regular poster board, especially in windy conditions.
o	Weatherproof: Consider if rain or sun will affect your signs. Paint or vinyl letters are more resilient than marker.
o	Double-sided signs: If possible, make your signs double-sided to maximize visibility from different angles, especially for media coverage.
•	Test Your Signs: Before the protest, hold up your signs and have someone view them from a distance similar to what you expect on the bridge. This will help you determine if the lettering is large enough and if the message is clear.
•	Spacing (Kerning): Ensure there is adequate space between letters and words so they don't blend together from a distance.
By focusing on large, bold, high-contrast lettering and concise messages, you'll maximize the impact and readability of your bridge protest signs.

title: New Member Orientation! (Summer Series)
description:
As a member-led youth movement, MOVE Texas Members are at the heart of our mission to transform democracy in Texas and beyond. **Born out of the student organizing movement in San Antonio in 2013,** MOVE Texas was founded by young people who saw a gap in civic engagement and decided to take action. What started as a small group of student leaders registering their peers to vote has since grown into a statewide movement of young people that trains, mobilizes, and empowers a new generation of progressive community organizers.

## Who are MOVE Texas Members?

MOVE Texas members are the backbone of the organization, reflecting the energy and diversity of young Texans leading the charge for a more just and equitable future for all Texans across race, class, and place.  As a youth movement, MOVE Texas members are under 30, and are either:


- **Students:** The original foundation of MOVE Texas—young leaders organizing on campuses across the state, running voter registration drives, educating their peers, and leading local issue-based campaigns.

- **Community Members:** Young Texans who are inspired by MOVE Texas’ mission and actively work to build power in their neighborhoods, from hosting events to advocating for direct local and statewide policy change.

## MOVE Texas members receive:

- Access to MOVE trainings, programs, and resources,

- Voting power for statewide and local campaigns,

- Exclusive invitations to MOVE statewide events,

- Connection to a network of peers organizing across the state,

- Exclusive members merch.


MOVE Texas membership is open to anyone who believes in the power of young people to lead and shape the future AND our present. **By becoming a member, you’re not just supporting a movement—you are the movement.**
